newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: Dutch pull the plug on wheat futures contract.
newsitem.headline: Dutch pull the plug on wheat futures contract.

text.p: The Amsterdam Agricultural Futures Exchange (ATA) said on Friday it had pulled the plug on its moribund wheat futures contract due to dismal participation.
"The contracts have been stopped due to a lack of interest, we do not know when they will re-start," a spokesman for the exchange told Reuters.
Since their launch in June, the contracts for milling wheat futures have consistently failed to match turnover expectations. On some days recently, volume has been nil.
Trade sources said earlier that a note had been handed out to brokers on the ATA floor explaining the cessation, adding they thought there would be no trade for a number of months.
"It's not surprising. There was no market for it, using Chicago was more liquid, more easy to use," one trade source said. "Market conditions have not been favourable.
The ATA could not say when the contracts would be re-launched because of its impending incorporation into the city's new exchange organisation Amsterdam Exchanges (AEX).
Amsterdam's stock, options and agricultural futures exchanges will merge on January 1 next year in a move aimed at bolstering the capital's position in a borderless post-EMU European market.

As recently as last week the ATA said it had no plans to scrap the contracts, but confirmed it was engaged in a process of re-evaluation. It said it was studying proposals to change some of their specifications concentrating on quality and lot size.
The Dutch contract is mark-denominated and trades lots of 125 tonnes.
"We have been carrying out an investigation with industry members and the trade to see what we can do to encourage more interest," ATA spokesman Robert Muller said last week.
He said some quality restrictions may be relaxed to allow more milling wheat from Europe's farmers on to the exchange.

In the early part of the year a race to set up Europe-wide wheat futures contracts developed between the ATA and other continental exchanges as speculative interest boomed on the world's premier grain exchange -- Chicago.
The Dutch managed to steal a march on its closest rival, the Paris MATIF, launching its contracts a month ahead in June after the French exchange found itself blocked by legal obstacles.
In the early stages, the ATA blamed the lack of participation on the timing of the launch, coming in between harvests, but the problem persisted, sparking the investigation.
But the main problem facing the ATA was one of dwindling speculative interest in grain markets world-wide.
"The main thing you need for success is a volatile cash market and we haven't had that recently," Muller added.
